pages.x: Most Rwandans were Hutu; about one in seven were Tutsi. Belgian rulers had favoured the Tutsi and made everyone carry an identity card naming their group. After independence Hutu governments took power, and waves of violence drove hundreds of thousands of Tutsi abroad. In 1990 Tutsi exiles of the Rwandan Patriotic Front invaded from Uganda.

As the war went on, extremists close to the government armed and trained militias called the Interahamwe, those who attack together, and a radio station, RTLM, poured out hatred, calling Tutsi inyenzi, cockroaches. In 1993 the government and the rebels signed a peace deal at Arusha, and UN peacekeepers arrived to watch over it.

On the evening of 6 April 1994 the plane carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down as it came in to land at Kigali, killing everyone aboard. Who fired the missiles is still disputed. Within hours soldiers and militias set up roadblocks and began to kill, working from lists of Tutsi and of Hutu who opposed them.

For about a hundred days neighbours killed neighbours, mostly with machetes and clubs. People who fled to churches, schools and stadiums were massacred there by the thousand, and militias checked identity cards at roadblocks. Hundreds of thousands of women were raped. Some Hutu hid Tutsi at the risk of their lives.
pages.of: people murdered, most of them Tutsi

pages.x: The UN commander, General Roméo Dallaire of Canada, had warned in January that a slaughter was being planned, but was told not to act. After ten Belgian peacekeepers were murdered, most of his force was pulled out. The world's powers even avoided the word genocide, which would have obliged them to act.

The genocide ended only as the Rwandan Patriotic Front, led by Paul Kagame, fought its way across the country. It took Kigali on 4 July, now Liberation Day, and its soldiers also carried out revenge killings. Fearing reprisals, about two million Hutu, among them many of the killers, fled abroad, most into Zaire, where cholera swept the refugee camps.

A UN court in Tanzania tried the leaders, and in 1998 it gave the first verdict of genocide ever reached by an international court. In Rwanda, with its prisons overflowing, village courts called gacaca, meeting on the grass, heard almost two million cases. Many killers now live beside the families of the people they killed.

Rwanda has rebuilt itself, and is now one of Africa's safest and fastest-growing countries, though Kagame rules it tightly and critics are silenced. The genocide shamed the world that stood by. The Hutu militias who fled into Zaire helped set off wars in Congo that killed millions more.
pts: About 800,000 murdered in a hundred days
